articles.title: Will Microsoft Kill Day 1 Launches via Game Pass? After Word Leaks of Potential Changes, Xbox Says It Has Nothing 'To Announce Today'
articles.summary: Microsoft has insisted it's yet to "finalize" any changes to Xbox Game Pass, after a potential leak detailed plans to drop the inclusion of new titles from day one.
articles.body:
Microsoft has insisted it's yet to "finalize" any changes to Xbox Game Pass, after a potential leak detailed plans to drop the inclusion of new titles from day one.

Since the introduction of Game Pass, Xbox has repeatedly changed how day one game releases are included in the subscription — from the introduction of a more expensive Ultimate tier (and various pricing changes up and down for that), plus Call of Duty's exclusion last fall.

This week, word began to spread online that day one games would be ditched from Game Pass altogether as soon as next spring, as part of upcoming moves that seem designed to improve margins, while also offering the subscription at a slightly lower and more attractive price point.

The changes were first discussed by Slayven, a moderator on video game forum ResetEra who stated previously shared accurate plans of other past Game Pass changes.

According to Slayven, Microsoft will offer two Xbox Game Pass subscriptions going forward — with and without advertising. The former will cost $12.99 a month, while the latter will cost $19.99 or $239.99 annually.

For the option without ads, this results in a small $3/month saving — though with the caveat that day one games will no longer be available. Cloud streaming and a family plan option will now be separate bolt-on costs ($5.99/month each).

There's word of online multiplayer also being available as a separate charge, though the details here are a little unclear. In what sounds like a new form of the Xbox Game Pass Essential experience, you'll be able to pay just for online gameplay, or with access to a game library.

In response to these details hitting the internet, Forbes reporter Paul Tassi received a statement from a Microsoft spokesperson that notably did not discount the leak as incorrect. Instead, the statement merely suggests that final decisions on any change have not yet been made, and there is nothing concrete to confirm right now. Here's that statement in full:

Xbox boss Asha Sharma has previously discussed the potential for including advertising as a way to lower the price of services such as Game Pass, so its introduction next year is not too much of a surprise. There has also long been a sense that Microsoft has struggled to balance the books with its offer of day one games — as seen in the sky-high price that Game Pass Ultimate previously reached, as well as the subsequent decision to exclude Call of Duty instead.

Removing day one games from Game Pass would presumably make the service less of a loss leader, while encouraging far more Xbox owners to splash out on the games Microsoft has ploughed millions into making. But it would also be a huge loss to attraction of Game Pass, that would inevitably lead some fans to unsubscribe.

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

articles.title: The Transformers: The Movie Rolls Back into Cinemas for 40th Anniversary
articles.body:
Film fans with a penchant for the Transformers franchise are in for an unexpected treat this month, with the return of the highly influential animated feature, The Transformers: The Movie to cinemas on 17th September!

40 years on from its original theatrical release, Hasbro and Fathom Entertainment have joined forces for this beautifully restored 4K theatrical release, which you can also enjoy as an immersive 4DX release in the US and UK, in cinemas starting on 17th September.

But that’s not all! If you’re planning to catch the film, don’t rush for the exit when the credits roll, as afterwards there will be the premiere of a brand-new 12-minute animated short, “Optimus Prime: Awakening.” Not only does this offer fans a new chapter in the saga, it also features the final original voice performance by Peter Cullen (Optimus Prime) as Optimus Prime, alongside a new performance by Frank Welker (Megatron/Soundwave).

Beautifully, prior to his sad passing earlier this year, Cullen shared that this chance to return to the role had meant a great deal to him, seeing the project as a homecoming to a character he had crafted and evolved over decades. Welker echoed this sentiment, sharing that “Peter’s portrayal of Prime was born of his own personal beliefs; honesty, loyalty, and always insisting on doing the right thing…I will miss my friend, but that voice and his heart and values will always be part of Optimus Prime.”

With millions of fans worldwide, the Transformers franchise explores the ongoing battle of good versus evil as the Autobots go head to head with the Decepticons who are attempting to conquer the universe. The original animated film features an incredible stellar cast including Leonard Nimoy (Galvatron), Eric Idle (Wrek-Gar) and, incredibly, Orson Welles (Unicron) in his final film role, alongside the aforementioned Peter Cullen and Frank Welker.

Set in the distant future of 2005 (20 years after the original TV series’ second season) the film follows the Autobots, who are being hunted by Unicron, a Transformers robot the size of a planet. With their own home planet, Cybertron, having been conquered by the Decepticons, Optimus Prime must rally the team to fulfil their goal of protecting all life. One shall stand, and one shall fall…

Of course, since then, the franchise has become a true behemoth, with 11 movies, countless animated series, and more toys and treats than you can shake an Ion Blaster at. As all true fans will know, freedom is the right of all sentient beings and on Transformers Day (17th September) you can exercise that freedom to get yourself to the cinema and catch it for yourself. Tickets are already available at this link .

If you can’t wait until then, you can whet your whistles with the movie soundtrack’s “The Transformers: The Movie: The Reformatted Edition ” available on all major streaming platforms and to buy, including some very nice looking vinyl options. With iconic tracks from the original, the collection also includes the new single “Nothing’s Gonna Stand In Our Way” featuring Sebastian Bach who many would know as the frontman of 1980s hard rock band Skid Row.

As you would expect from a leading toy and game company like Hasbro, there’s also some cool new toys to accompany the release. Perfect for collectors, there’s an interactive electronic replica of the Autobot’s Matrix of Leadership alongside a range of studio series figures based on the 1986 movie. With an extendable frame that allows you to display it open or closed, it also includes LED lighting in its core, and the song “The Touch” by Stan Bush from the film. There’s also a great new range of action figures from established partner Studio Series.

If you want to keep abreast of all of this and more, you can follow @TransformersOfficial on Instagram and TikTok, and @Transformers on X and Facebook. For tickets, go here .

articles.title: Images for Unannounced Tiny Tina's Wonderlands and Brothers in Arms Games Leak Online
articles.summary: Development images for a Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands sequel and a new Brothers in Arms game have emerged online, amid reports both were scrapped.
articles.body:
Development images for a Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands sequel and a new Brothers in Arms game have emerged online, amid reports both were scrapped.

MP1st , which published the work-in-progress images, said the games were in development at former Embracer-owned studio Lost Boys Interactive, which returned to independence last year. Embracer sold Gearbox to 2K Games parent company Take-Two in 2024.

Lost Boys Interactive worked on the original Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands, a fantasy-themed spinoff of Gearbox’s hugely successful Borderlands franchise, as well as Borderlands 4, so it’s not a huge surprise to see evidence that it worked on the sequel.

Indeed, it was thought that Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands did so well commercially that a sequel was inevitable. In 2022, Gearbox chief Randy Pitchford called Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands a “major victory,” adding that the developer viewed it as a new franchise with “future experiences already under development.”

“Wonderlands shattered all of our target expectations, both critically and commercially,” said Pitchford during an Embracer Group annual general meeting, “and I'm thrilled to report that in addition to great financial rewards from this victory that will be coming our way in the coming quarters, we have established a firm beachhead, and we now clearly have a new franchise on our hands.”

However, since then, nothing has emerged on a new Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands game. Gearbox has yet to announce its next project following last year’s release of Borderlands 4 .

Meanwhile, the last mainline Brothers in Arms game was 2008’s Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway . A fourth game in the WW2 shooter series, Furious 4 , was cancelled and eventually turned into ill-fated hero shooter Battleborn . Pitchford has over the years indicated that a new Brothers in Arms game was on the way, but it never materialised.

The released images don’t really tell us much about the games themselves, other than they were in development. Were they canceled as part of Gearbox's sale to Take-Two? Are there new versions of each game in the works somewhere at Gearbox? IGN has asked for comment.

Wesley is Director, News at IGN. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

articles.title: Nintendo opens up Fire Emblem with the gigantic Fortune’s Weave
articles.summary: Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is an engrossing and huge strategy RPG for the Nintendo Switch 2.
articles.body: Nintendo has gotten quite good at making open-ended games. The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild upended the idea of what a Zelda game could be by giving the player free rein to tackle any part of the map, a philosophy iterated upon with Tears of the Kingdom. On the Switch 2 this idea expanded to Mario Kart World and Donkey Kong Bananza. Now, Nintendo has brought this philosophy to Fire Emblem with Fortune’s Weave. It works really well; with its many ways to progress through the game and tailor teams to your liking, Fortune’s Weave has become my favorite game on the Switch 2 so far. Fortune’s Weave’s structure is a big reason why it feels so open: Instead of locking you to one path, Fortune’s Weave is designed so that you can experience multiple stories in one massive playthrough. There are four main hero routes and a final act that ties things together, giving you several opportunities to start over from scratch and master the dizzying amount of mechanics and meta-strategy involved in winning fights and building up your group. From early on you can swap between heroes and storylines at will, and it’s even possible to merge stats from characters you use in multiple routes to make one supercharacter later. The systems go really deep, but Fortune’s Weave gives you many ways to customize things exactly to your liking. The game is split into a few sections. There’s a brief prologue that introduces the main protagonist and your mission to save the world and defeat an evil demon lord. To aid in your quest, you can recruit the four missing heroes from the recent past by playing through their individual stories in two parts. Part one features the hero of your choice as they compete in a grand tournament in the city of Dagsion, while part two carries over your hero’s squad to fight in a war. If you complete a hero’s path, you can take them and any of their allies into part three, where the true protagonist leads an effort to fight the undead. [Media: Parts one and three give you a lot of leeway to train up for battles and build your teams as you’d like. You’ll quickly fall into a rhythm of splitting time between the main story battles, running around Dagsion to prepare for fights, enlist allies, and explore a vast map to gather resources and fight in small skirmishes. There’s a calendar system that counts down the days toward the next main story event, but you have the freedom to spend your days however you’d like. I fell into a comforting pattern where I’d explore a map for one in-game week, come back to Dagsion to complete weekly activities like training up skills and sharing meals with people in town to build rapport, and then back head out to the map to tackle more quests or grind out some XP. (Part two is pretty much all about battles, as you’re mostly just playing one big fight after another with very little pre-battle prep.) The main battles are your typical Fire Emblem turn-based strategy. You can choose which allies you want to use, and then you spend each turn deciding how to best attack your enemies or buff your team with healing spells and other support moves. Each of your characters has a different class, and a diverse squad is key; as much as I’d love to run a team that consists just of flying units, if they came upon any archers, they’d probably be toast. Some battles have different objectives to mix things up, like tasking you with defeating thieves before they escape while simultaneously fighting giant birds. On the game’s standard difficulty, and with permadeath turned off, I didn’t have much trouble. But I often invoked the blessings of gods during battles, which give you handy abilities like rewinding back to a previous move if you make a mistake. There are also battles that play out like a more typical turn-based RPG, which you’ll run into in dungeons on the map and with occasional story battles. I found these much less interesting than the strategy battles, and thanks to an autoplay feature, I usually skipped them altogether to get the experience and stat boosts. I chose to finish all four hero routes in parts one and two so that I could bring them into part three. It was a herculean effort: Completing each hero’s path took me about 100 hours in total. And that was after reducing battle animations, skipping cutscenes I had already seen, and doing a lot of fast traveling. But with each hero’s playthrough, I better understood how to train characters, assign them advanced classes to build balanced teams, and use resources from the map to make my weapons more powerful. Part three also adds one extra complication: Instead of roaming the map with a single character and their team, you can juggle multiple squads at a time. This initially felt daunting, but I quickly settled into deploying my squads to different corners of the map to finish quests, leveling up my whole team, and crushing a lot of bad guys. [Image: Not every hour of my playthrough, which ended at about 130 hours, was well spent. In parts one and two, I repeated a lot of quests, cutscenes, and exploration. Part two features the same levels, just with the characters swapped around depending on which hero you’re playing as. In part three, managing multiple squads simultaneously can feel like you’re inching across the map. And the strange, leery tea party minigame from Three Houses returns as “bird time,” where you talk with and “observe” other characters as the game’s main protagonist — who has taken the form of a bird — to build support. I promise the bird form makes sense in the context of the story, but it’s still weird. But even with the repetition, I found myself completely immersed in Fortune’s Weave. The loop of leveling up my characters, preparing for battle, and routing my enemies was nearly perfect, and I couldn’t get enough. Reaching part three in particular felt like a significant reward for my hard work; after 100 hours, I was thrilled when I could bring all of my teams together for the final push. Fortune’s Weave is just the latest example of how Nintendo adapts the idea of openness in a way that makes sense for each franchise. In this case, it doesn’t change the core game like how Breath of the Wild transformed Zelda. Instead, the game’s open-ended nature adds even more layers of strategy to a series that had already started pushing its own boundaries with titles like Three Houses. Fortune’s Weave feels like the culmination of what Nintendo has been building Fire Emblem to be. Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave launches on the Nintendo Switch 2 on September 17th.

articles.title: Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave Is Among the Best Games This Series Has Seen, With Compelling Stories Spread Across a Huge, Branching Campaign
articles.summary: An excellent combination of combat strategy, time management, and compelling stories.
articles.body:
The Fire Emblem series has always prided itself on how it teaches you to become a master tactician on the battlefield, using its turn-based battle system to push you to truly think strategically. In its more recent games, strategy became an important aspect not just while waging war, but between battles as well: How will you make the most of your time before the next skirmish? Who needs extra training, or perhaps a nice shared meal to increase camaraderie? Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave doesn’t just take the next step down that path, it makes an ambitious leap forward. It expands the scope of how you manage your budding heroes and explore its unexpectedly engaging map, and introduces some of the most harrowing and clever battles I’ve seen in the series to date. Its branching story intertwines into a grand epic that always seemed to have a new twist up its sleeve, and even after a hundred hours, I’ve still got more unique paths to tread that I’m itching to dive back into. Like a gladiator risking it all, Fortune’s Weave never stops aiming for the top – and it rarely misses that mark.

This story begins with an undead apocalypse already in progress, but while your customizable character is asked to stop it, you’ll soon learn that salvation is only to be found in the past. Thanks to some very on-brand time travel shenanigans, you must go back and ensure four legendary heroes survive the trials and tribulations that surround a series of colosseum matches known as the Heroic Games, each with their own path full of distinct, large-scale battles. 2019’s Fire Emblem: Three Houses similarly let you choose your own story path, but its first act played out largely the same before the second diverged depending on your faction choice. Fortune’s Weave not only flips that structure on its head, it also manages to make its finale more robust and impactful depending on how much of its main cast you reach the last act with.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave Gameplay Screenshots

This works thanks in large part to a single save file system that helps funnel each path toward one merged conclusion. I’ll admit that I had my reservations at first, as just one save slot initially seemed to limit replayability. However, Fortune’s Weave has a surprisingly good solution for managing these multiple paths. A nifty little hub room allows you to not only pick which story path you want to progress at almost any time, but even go back and replay any chapter you’ve done, no matter which act it’s in. Looking back will give you a snapshot of the army you had at the beginning of that chapter, who you’d recruited, and how strong they were – and if you choose to redo it, the snapshot for the following chapter will update with any differences, allowing you to keep progressing along this new playthrough without wiping data from any subsequent chapters further down the line that you’d already completed. It’s a smart way to weave the time travel theme into a mechanic that would be invaluable regardless, and lets you see nearly everything Fortune’s Weave has to offer without having to start from scratch on a new playthrough.

Each story path is wonderfully unique, offering different glimpses of life in the Dagdan Empire: Cai, the exuberant country kid in over his head as he tries to find a way to rescue his father from execution; Dietrich, the detached (and slightly unhinged) swordsman from a distant land who really only cares about finding worthy opponents for his blade; Theodora, queen of a southern kingdom seeking relief and acceptance for her people; and Leda, a talented musician and dancer on a quest for revenge against her father’s murderers. Each has an intriguing tale to tell as their personal quests lead them to the empire’s sprawling capital, Dagsion (imagine Rome if it was literally ruled over by the pantheon of gods), and I loved discovering the larger conspiracy lurking beneath it all as their journeys start to intertwine.

These four heroes are initially out to win the grand Heroic Games and win their heart's desire, but I was delighted to see how the paths they take to get there all have their own twists and turns. Rather than treading the exact same ground, each branch had me alternate between colosseum matches and more personal storylines. I’m happy I chose to play as Leda first, as her tale of vengeance was a wild ride to watch unfold. The story doesn’t shy away from how badly her desire for revenge affects those around her (which is spurred on by a cursed instrument she carries), and even though things never get as dark as they could have, she isn’t above gleefully describing to people how much they’d suffer if they got in her way.

I also came to admire how each of the paths in Fortune’s Weave are their own specific strands on a larger web of intrigue. It’s not exactly a new concept to have a secretive evil group pulling strings from the shadows, but it's the way each hero uncovers certain pieces of their motives and operations that compelled me the most. It never felt like I was stumbling through the dark trying to figure out what was going on, but more that each path provided new context to the events that were unfolding, which then leads to a dramatic twist in act two that was quite effective.

When stacked against these champions and their quests, my own character (who defaults to the name Eshmel) came off a little lackluster at first… but oddly enough, I didn’t really mind that. Compared to Byleth from Three Houses, who constantly fought for my attention between the other main characters, Fortune’s Weave is wise to put Eshmel in the background for the first half of the story while the others establish themselves, only swooping in at critical moments with their best Tuxedo Mask impression to ensure the heroes survive until the present day. Otherwise, Eshmel is content to chill out in town disguised in the form of a cute, plump little bird that everyone seems to love. In the final act, they take on a more commander-in-chief role, and though they end up sharing a lot of moments with the goddess helping you achieve your goals, their main role is support – and it’s something they do very well, bolstering your chosen squad with their incredible powers.

While their smaller role is ultimately a smart choice, it is a shame that Eshmel is largely silent outside of a few specific sequences, mostly chiming in through inconsequential dialogue choices accompanied by a simple, non-verbal gesture. Given how good the voice acting is across the whole cast, I didn’t really feel like I gained anything from these attempts at roleplay (aside from occasionally having companions interact with me in bird form, and then trying to pick the appropriate bird-response so I could… observe them… you know what, never mind).

Still, the visuals have improved greatly overall, from fluid zoom-ins as characters clash to the briefly animated and expressive character portraits during dialogue. Even sprinting or warping around the major hub city loads way faster than Garreg Mach Monastery in Three Houses. I still wish some scenes that weren’t cinematics had a bit of their own flair – I can only watch the screen fade to black and then have a single slice effect cut through it to signify someone did something with a weapon so many times. Thankfully, there are plenty of entertaining cutscenes saved for the bigger moments.

The meat of any Fire Emblem game is its tactical turn-based combat, and Fortune’s Weave does not disappoint on that front. Building off of Three Houses, the classic weapon triangle is replaced by other advantages and weaknesses ready to exploit on the battlefield. Little touches, like lances dealing more damage to cavalry or fist weapons making units more evasive, are just the tip of a strategic iceberg that got me to think differently. As my army clashed and my units increased in power, so too did their repertoire of combat arts and skills, adding increased power, evasion, or even the ability to stun and confuse opponents at the cost of a weapon’s durability.

One of the best additions to this battle math takes the form of incredibly rare swords that can cleave through undead enemies that would otherwise receive reduced damage from most sources. As I started to encounter more and more of the undead, figuring out who to bestow these weapons upon and where to deploy them became critical to my survival. At one point, I had a small squad fending off attacks from all sides, with their lone magical blade trading hands from one fighter to the next each turn so everyone had a fighting chance. Managing them is a cool wrinkle to consider that’s also full of thematic flavor.

Even though most battle maps have fairly standard objectives – take out leaders, rout the entire enemy force, etc. – plenty of the main missions throw some increasingly nasty curveballs at you. They continually forced me to adapt my tactics on the fly, reform my lines to deal with unexpected threats, and keep my team mobile to avoid new hazards and obstacles that appear all over the place. Rarely could I be complacent enough to slowly move across the map and let the enemy army slam into me bit by bit. Instead, I had to juggle split up squads, make risky strikes into well-defended territory, and ensure no one got left behind in the process.

My favorite addition by far is the introduction of a handful of cursed artifacts and the Blaze Arts they bestow upon many of the main characters. Their inclusion not only changed how I approached every battle, but made each of the four story paths even more unique. These cursed objects can let Cai launch a flame blast to hit several units, or let Dietrich teleport through barriers to close the distance on foes who thought themselves safe. I was very glad to have Leda on my first playthrough, as her ability to play a cursed instrument can buff a large number of allies at once, and her repertoire eventually expands to a song that gives everyone the ability to negate that undead defense bonus that had given me so much trouble.

There’s a clever and ever-building risk/reward system tied to these artifacts, as using Blaze Arts costs a bit of HP, which could easily leave my heroes exposed to a killing blow. These arts (along with using other cursed weapons and artifacts) increases a blaze gauge that boosts a unit’s stats when filled halfway… but reduces their maximum HP for the rest of the battle if the gauge fills completely. As the story continues to expand, so too do the opportunities to use these arts in some really exciting and strategic ways that I did not expect, making it more and more tempting to put lives on the line to ensure my team’s overall survival.

While Fortune’s Weave starts off fairly tame, the difficulty ramps up by the end of its first act, which took me about 50 hours to finish. Foes start to appear with better weapons than I could muster, promoted to even more advanced classes. By its much more condensed second act, I was running into all sorts of trouble, forcing me to turn to the gods for help. Expanding on a time rewinding feature first introduced in Three Houses, you can now invoke a god’s blessing to try things differently if your units start to drop – but Fortune’s Weave has built upon this idea with the ability to earn blessings from multiple gods.

Aside from the time rewind function, blessings can only be used one per turn in exchange for finite resources. I was able to literally pray to the gods of RNG to grant my team temporary bonuses like increased hit chance, evasion, and damage absorption to survive until the next round. This is entirely optional, of course, but it’s not just some “easy mode” crutch meant to entirely negate the difficulty. You’ll need to be smart to equip the right blessings before each battle starts, and know when to spend your limited currency to avert an incoming disaster and snatch victory from the impending jaws of defeat.

Much of my time between battles was spent wandering the streets of the capital city of Dagsion, and while it’s not exactly crowded, it does have a fair amount of hustle and bustle. I could explore the temples of the gods, mingle with the other gladiatorial hopefuls to scout potential recruits, and partake in other activities like weapon skill training or sharing meals while waiting for the next main mission. Unlike Three Houses, your exploration isn’t limited to just a few free days per month – instead, each day was mine to do as I pleased, and the more my renown grew across the land, the more facilities I gained access to.

Time won’t pass just by training your units or sitting in the bathhouse, however, for the open road is where adventure truly lies. A sprawling map of the continent is laid out for you to explore like a grand board game, and in it hides a surprisingly deep layer of strategy and time management as you uncover roads that lead to points of interest across every corner of the land. Those include spots to feast or forage for supplies, random bands of enemies to test your mettle against, towns to visit and trade with for valuable gear, and small dungeons to delve into teeming with riches and upgrades. Four steps across the map costs one turn (which translates to a fourth of a full day), and the more I uncovered, the more I realized how important planning out my travels were given the campaign’s limited timeframe.

With anywhere from a few weeks to over a month between rounds in the Heroic Games, it was a fun challenge to juggle uncovering spots on the map that led me toward sidequest markers with finding the right moment to make my way back to the capital in time for certain special events – like spectating other teams in the competition to gain skill experience. I soon found myself eagerly devising plans for each of my outings across the world, looking for ways I could knock out a few nearby quest markers as I uncovered a new region.

If that somehow wasn’t enough, each hero has unique exploration skills that fundamentally changed how I planned my expeditions. Theodora, for instance, is the only hero who can recruit battalions at towns and employ them in battle to unleash devastating area of effect attacks (something your enemies will start doing even if your chosen hero cannot), while only Cai can find spots to tame wild animals to serve as personalized rides for mounted units, giving them additional stat boosts the more they bond with their ride.

Since many of the activities both in the city and out in the world replenish each week, there was more motivation to bounce back and forth between the two and divide my time as best I could. That said, the allure of a giant, ever-expanding map often proved too enticing to ignore, and I happily allowed myself to be distracted from returning to “home base” in favor of uncovering new ground — especially with so many hidden dungeons to find.

Unlike the traditional top down skirmishes found elsewhere, dungeons build off of ideas first introduced way back in Shadows of Valentia for the 3DS. You pick a small group of five from your larger army when you enter one, and each is teeming with enemies you can either sneak and dash around or lunge toward to initiate combat. These clashes are more akin to a battle you’d see in a classic JRPG, with both teams forming a line and alternating attacks. Though it’s a fairly simplified system, there are short bursts of fun to be had here, almost like a minigame.

Just like in the larger battles, picking the right fighter to attack against an opposing unit that is poised to retaliate can be the difference between cleaving off a chunk of your team’s shared HP and negating their strike with the right foil. I’ll admit, early on it sometimes came down to just having a highly defensive tank in the party to soak all incoming blows – but as the difficulty ramped up, so too did the enemy variety. Thankfully, the ability to link up attacks or have one ally heal while another struck out meant my group could survive even longer in these dungeons, allowing me to find cool treasures like those cursed weapons.

It’s not truly a Fire Emblem game unless you’re slowly building an army out of a rag-tag crew of miscreants from all walks of life, and while Fortune’s Weave doesn’t break from that tradition entirely, it opts for a slightly different approach. By the time each of the four main heroes reaches the Heroic Games at Dagsion, they’ll have their own small crew of (mostly) trusted allies. But the colosseum fights are much bigger skirmishes, and you’ll need to bolster your ranks if you want to survive. As luck would have it, wandering the capital can feel a bit like window shopping for the deadliest mercenaries in the land.

Almost every potential recruit has their own conditions that need to be met before they’ll agree to join your group. Most will want you to have achieved a certain level of renown from questing, but you’ll have to build enough support so that they trust you as well, a process that involves things like taking them out for fine dining or to the theater. Some may even have a final negotiation to resolve, like handing over certain items or money (one character actually quizzed me on the region to see if I’d been paying attention in my exploration). Fortune’s Weave even cleverly mixes up these requirements depending on who you’re playing as, and some may not want to join certain characters at all, giving you an extra incentive to explore other story paths. This creates another fun wrinkle in the time management between missions, as I had to ensure I was properly scouting recruits who were the best fit for my team and allocating time to spend with them while in the capital (as well as finding gifts for them while traveling abroad).

I was unsure about this system at the start, especially what it meant for the overarching story. Picking up random mercenaries at unpredictable points means they don’t really add much to the main story (though you can still unlock your fair share of support conversations with them). Instead, each hero usually trades words with only the small group they form at the start of their story during important moments, which makes everyone else feel less important. However, I soon realized this approach works out for the better for a few reasons.

For one, it allows for a more intimate story to unfold, without having to worry about some random bandit I picked up chiming in with something thoughtful. The second reason I did not anticipate is that it makes room for your main gladiator “rivals” to shine. It’s not just the four champions you choose from that are in the running to be crowned winner of the Heroic Games, as you’ll soon spot other teams around the capital led by some pretty charismatic characters.

Much like how each story path touches on different aspects of the main antagonists, you’ll also have different interactions with the other team leaders. Early on, you’re even able to team up with some of them during qualifying rounds to get a taste of their power, and it turns out they’re just as capable as you. I really enjoyed getting to temporarily command leaders like the laser gun-toting Anatolia (no, I will not elaborate) or the mask-wearing priestess Orchel, as they had their own unique spin on Blaze Arts that differed greatly from any of the main heroes. (My only slight disappointment stemmed from getting spoiled on one character’s mysterious backstory by… their own info page, which described their true nature while they were a guest in my party, before it was formally revealed.)

These rivals become more formidable when it's your turn to face off against them, and depending on which story path you’re on, it’s even possible to help them out with special missions after they drop out of the Heroic Games. These “paralogues” might be low in quantity, but they were all extremely fun and challenging. My favorite included helping one character escort civilians out of a map dominated by a giant beast summoning tentacles all over the place – getting everyone out alive forced me to be extremely precise, stunning the ridiculously powerful creature at just the right moments while I made a break for the exit. Completing these paralogues also had some pretty great and far-reaching effects on the story at large, which once again made the idea of going back to see the ones on another path all the more enticing.

With so much to consider and plan around outside of combat, it’s easy to get overwhelmed and lose sight of your immediate objectives. At one point, I felt myself starting to get torn as I tried to do everything at once, which is when the true appeal of Fortune’s Weave became clear to me. It’s better to think of its story not as a five-course meal you need to march through as you try and finish everything, but rather as an all-you-can-eat buffet. You’re not expected to eat the entire buffet!

Instead, I focused on exactly what I wanted: recruiting a handful of characters that caught my eye, doing weapon training whenever I happened to be back in town to promote my units to better classes, maybe giving away a few gifts, and trying to complete a few quests out in the world before coming back to town. Anyone I didn’t end up recruiting would still be there for another story path, and the same was true of any dungeons I didn’t uncover or the far reaches of the map I didn’t have time to travel to. I was always allowed to be as comprehensive or as relaxed as I wanted to be. Sure, exploring a mine could mean I find materials to refine or repair weapons to use more combat arts, but I could also just use those arts more sparingly, and then spend that time leveling my units until the next mission to compensate.

Fortune’s Weave even extends that freedom of choice to its second act in a pretty wild way, though I’ll avoid specific spoilers. As the story escalates, whichever hero you’ve progressed with most is drawn into a string of intimidating, large-scale battles where the calendar and exploration elements are removed. It’s a much more condensed arc, and its battles become incredibly grueling across maps that are much larger than those in the first act. What surprised me is that entering this second part of the story informed me that I could opt to skip it entirely , which would then auto-level my units appropriately for act three and provide a TL:DR version of how the story advanced.

Along with being able to replay these missions whenever I wanted, the ability to skip them outright is a pretty thoughtful one for subsequent playthroughs using different heroes… but I was a little shocked it gave me this option on my first run. I, of course, declined this offer, and was much happier flexing my strategic muscles on these satisfyingly tough battles (though that happiness turned to outright horror around the time I found myself staring down four giant war elephants on a bridge, all charging in my direction).

Brendan's Favorite Fire Emblem Games Ranked

All of this leads to Fortune’s Weave’s final act, and while I still won’t delve into plot details, it’s worth touching lightly on just how insane things get. It took me around 70 hours to reach this point, and the momentum could have easily become a slow shamble to the finish line as it retreads familiar ground. And yet, it wasn’t until this point – when all of the individual stories merged into one – that Fortune’s Weave evolved from a great adventure into a truly phenomenal RPG.

The way its grand world map is recontextualized from something I had spent countless hours exploring into a centerpiece for tactical warfare gave me an immense thrill. This section had smart answers ready for how I could best make use of an army that had grown awfully crowded (regardless of how many or how few individual story paths I had completed by that point). It introduces not only great new methods to manage those troops, but does so in a way where nobody was truly left without a purpose, and it encouraged as much multi-tasking as I wanted to delve into (and man did I ever delve). In nearly every respect, it was the perfect culmination of strategy and management that I had been honing over the course of this story, providing just as many challenges as new tools to overcome them. Even Eshmel finally gets their chance to shine, using their otherworldly power to lead the charge.

Truthfully, I probably spent way more time than needed doing everything I could before the final showdown, but I never once felt compelled to simply run down the clock. There were so many ways I wanted to optimize my forces, and even then my adversaries were definitely not taking it easy on me. These final missions tested the limit of my ability to see all my allies safely through to the end thanks to some downright devious battlefields filled with punishing traps, and I wouldn’t have a high-stakes conclusion be any other way.

articles.title: Fire Emblem Fortune's Weave Review, Gameplay Impressions, Videos and Features
articles.summary: Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is the most epic and grand blockbuster exclusive to hit the Nintendo Switch 2.
articles.body:
Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is the most epic and grand blockbuster exclusive to hit the Nintendo Switch 2.

Fortune's Weave is an impressive refinement of the Fire Emblem formula and easily the most accessible release in the series. Featuring incredible tactics gameplay, endearing characters and a story worth seeing every bit, Fortune's Weave is a generation-defining, must-play masterpiece for all gamers and a true contender for Game of the Year.

Fire Emblem boasts exceptional turn-based, tactical role-playing gameplay and Fortune's Weave expands the formula to be even more satisfying and rewarding. The primary battle encounters tasks players with navigating a grid-based environment where each character can move a certain number of spaces and perform a specific task, such as attacking or healing. It is strategic greatness that will have players often agonizing over every decision in order to achieve the optimal path of success.

In Fortune's Weave, gamers will control four unique main playable characters (Cai, Dietrich, Theodora and Leda) across an interwoven story that is the most engaging and expansive tale from an exclusive on Switch 2. It is absolutely worth seeing each arc to the fullest to gain a better sense of each character and the story. It's impressive how each arc provides different perspectives to key characters and pivotal moments, which also helps build intrigue and mystery while playing an arc.

A key feature allows players to switch to different arcs to advance chapter by chapter across the four perspectives, or simply play one arc to completion at a time. It's a fascinating decision, but most importantly, ensures that players have agency in how they want to advance the story and ensures that players won't miss key aspects.

Each of the four main characters have unique character traits, weapon proficiencies and Blaze Arts, which is one of the coolest combat features associated with the main characters. As gamers progress, they'll recruit new allies to join their squad in each story arc. There are tons of different weapons, skills, classes and characters to unlock, many of which feature unique aspects that will completely change the way players approach each battle.

As players improve characters, they'll unlock different Combat Arts for their weapons that provide great damage output at the cost of a weapon's finite durability. However, it is the Blaze Arts that really help set Fortune's Weave apart from others titles. Blaze Arts introduce an intriguing risk-reward mechanic during battles as gamers must decide if they want to sacrifice a portion of that character's health in order to gain a major perk for that turn or an upcoming turn. During battles, the decision to use a normal attack, Combat Art or Blaze Art really enhances the strategic nature of an already engaging gameplay system as players will scrutinize every decision they make en route to victory... or defeat.

Thankfully, one of the other elements during combat is the access to Blessings from the different Gods. There are several Blessings to unlock, and even level up for additional perks. For example, Fortuna's blessing allows players to rewind to previous turns during battle and is by far one of the best features in the game as it is often a saving grace before defeat. Of course, players can choose not to rewind or use any other blessing they unlock if they want a more traditional experience but the rewind feature is easily one of the best possible features for a strategy game.

Although Fortuna's blessing is free to use, using a Blessing from another God costs in-game currency called Divine Sand, which is limited to a specific number of uses per cycle. The different Blessings are a great expansion of the in-battle perk system. Fortuna's blessing, for example, is especially useful in Fire Emblem as players can choose their difficulty options, with the traditional experience meaning that if a character is defeated during battle, they're gone for good compared to the casual difficulty where fallen characters revive for the next battle.

Fortune's Weave features great level designs, especially during the main quest as environments are varied and some battles even have specific win conditions to break up the flow of combat and add new elements of strategy. Maps also feature unique characteristics that impact battle, such as different terrain or elevation. For example, if a character is on a spot with a bush, they'll have an increased chance to dodge an incoming attack. Different classes will have different advantages based on the terrain, and there's also flying mounts that can travel over water or have an elevated advantage, for example. In addition to the intriguing level designs, the battle theme music is also excellent.

Where Fortune's Weave differs from some recent Fire Emblem games and other tactics game is the turn-based encounters in dungeons that resemble turn-based gameplay most commonly found in JRPGs like Final Fantasy, or even previously seen in Fire Emblem Echoes: Shadows of Valentia. Given how massive the game is, these traditional turn-based encounters serve as a great way to mix up the gameplay and add another element to the pacing to keep the game refreshing. These dungeons are excellent opportunities to find loot and level up characters in battles against various types of monsters and enemies.

Should players want to try to speedrun the game or have an itch to advance to the next intriguing story bit, there's an auto-battle option for each type of combat encounter. If a battle is lost, gamers can choose to restart from before battle, at a certain point in battle or from the beginning of battle, with the option of retaining any experience gained up until the moment of defeat. This is by far one of the best quality-of-life features available as it softens the blow of restarting a battle from the beginning and allows players to keep improving their squad if they went into a battle feeling underleveled. This fantastic feature should be implemented into more role-playing games to prevent frustration.

Another quality-of-life feature during the grid-based battles is the option to adjust battle animations. For example, players can choose to watch flashy and stylish animated attacks unfold for each individual encounter during the grand-scale battle. If players decide they want to limit the animations for time or speedrun purposes, they can limit how expansive the animations are, even to the point of not seeing them at all. Given the magnitude of the game and the general release calendar in gaming, it's a necessary option that is sure to be beloved by many gamers.

Despite its massive size, Fortune's Weave still manages to respect the player's time. It's constantly expanding at a gradual pace, managing to keep mysteries of the story present and intriguing, while also incorporating new mechanics to keep gameplay fresh across all of the story arcs. There's many quality-of-life features that help decrease the amount of time required to complete certain tasks.

For example, between battles players can explore the city and open world. There are tasks specific to the open world, such as searching for materials, battling enemies, capturing wildlife and recruiting soldiers. While exploring the open world to complete specific tasks, each action takes a turn and there's only so many turns available to the player until the next main story mission. If a player chooses not to engage with the open world in totality, they have an option in the city to automatically advance a specific number of turns and accomplish certain tasks, such as leveling up a character's total experience, leveling up a character's class-specific experience or searching for loot and gold. It's just a smart mechanic for gamers who wish to advance a bit quicker to the main quest.

Another excellent quality-of-life feature that ensure the player's time is respected is that the game will automatically complete side quests for one character if the player already completed that quest by another character in a different story arc, which will then provide in-game currency, Renown, experience and items. There are also overall game tasks that can be completely across all characters that will unlock new featured, one of them being able to increase experience gain by reaching certain milestones in progress.

Each main character also has a unique task fit for their personality and motives, which keeps the four paths feeling fresh, in order to increase their Renown. For example, Theodora can recruit non-playable soldiers that she can deploy at specific spots on the map to search for loot, Cai can farm for materials and capture horses, Leda can put on performances to unlock Blaze Arts and Dietrich is on the hunt to battle enemies. Renown is important to build up during each arc as it unlocks perks along the way, including the important option of taking an exam for a new, improved class. By taking a certification exam for a more advanced class, each character can improve their base stats and learn new skills.

In the city, players can train characters at the arena to improve skills, unlock new classes, have meals with other characters and give gifts to characters to improve relationships, plus more activities that unlock over the course of the game. Giving gifts and having meals with other characters is essential to increasing their support with the main playable character within each arc in order to eventually recruit them to the party. The support system is a mainstay in the Fire Emblem series and is important here in order to build out the squad with as many allies as possible.

Fortune's Weave is among the deepest, most intense and most mature stories in Nintendo's vast library. The four main characters have clearly-defined motives and developer Intelligent Systems does a great job pacing each chapter of the four story arcs, ensuring players can quickly get invested in each character from the beginning and then forming a long-lasting bond with each character, and their companions, by the end of their arc. Characters, even beyond the main leads, are endearing, charming and have unique personalities. Over dozens of hours of gameplay, players will learn about their motives, quirks, humor and distinct characteristics. There's fantastic voice acting, especially for the main characters but also the supporting cast. Each character is distinct with easily-identifiable voices. However, the main characters, especially the actresses for Theodora and Leda, do phenomenal work to get the player invested in their motives and back stories.

Players can listen to exhilarating music from the soundtrack in the menu but one amazing feature, which more games should add, is the ability to rewatch cutscenes and events from a menu. Many of these are epic cutscenes worth watching many times again, so it's awesome to be able to see them without having to replay the entire game.

Among other accessibility and quality-of-life options, there's a text log to keep track of dialogue and the tons of side quests. Inside dungeons, there's an icon showing how many unopened chests are left when roaming dungeons. There's also options to toggle game speed, fast forward through certain scenes and animations, fast travel to specific locations in the city and even mask insectile enemies for phobias. With the advanced hardware of Switch 2, there's extremely fast loading through the game and players can even choose to use mouse controls if they feel more comfortable than the traditional controller setup. Overall, Fortune's Weave runs flawlessly and is truly the complete package for an epic tale.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is a monumental release for the series and Switch 2. It features arguably the best voice acting and cinematics seen in a Nintendo game. The movie-quality art design, music and epic cutscenes are feats pushing Switch 2 to the next level in Year 2.

Gamers can easily sink in hundreds of hours of gameplay due to the vast nature of the story and how many permutations there are with different characters and gameplay elements. It is the peak of the series, impressively managing to surpass recent favorites like Three Houses and Awakening. The progression system doesn't overwhelm the player with mechanics at the start but gradually layers new systems and techniques at a nice pace during the story.

Fortune's Weave is the culmination of decades Nintendo spent refining aspects of the formula to literally weave them into one complete package. The presentation style is near flawless with distinct chapters, access to tons of characters, excellent menus, easy-to-follow tips and a lot of accessibility options. The expansive lore, carefully-crafted world-building and fascinating characters are sure to hook players from beginning to end of this unpredictable, grand journey featuring one of the best stories in the franchise.

The story, character development, art style, music, accessibility, and most importantly, gameplay all come together to create an experience that will stick with gamers for years to come and have many immediately dreaming about more. Easily one of the best games of a stacked year, Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave deserves to be nominated for Game of the Year with the very best of the bunch.

articles.title: 30th Anniversary Pokémon Trading Card Launch Sparks Enormous Queues, 'Ghost Chairs' Criticism, and Price Hikes
articles.summary: Pokémon's coveted 30th anniversary trading card set has gone on sale, though its launch has seen some stores jacking up prices, while long lines of customers have camped outside overnight.
articles.body:
Pokémon's coveted 30th anniversary trading card set has gone on sale, though its launch has seen some stores jacking up prices, while long lines of customers have camped outside overnight.

High demand and a limited supply have impacted every recent Pokémon card release, but huge attention is being paid to this launch in particular due to its nostalgic re-release of beloved cards, as well as some ultra rare new designs.

Of course, much of this demand is driven by the lucrative resale market, with a quick profit to be made online when flogging unopened boxes or rare individual cards. Some retailers have started to limit individual purchase amounts, or even cut open packaging to destroy cards' resale value . In Japan, facial recognition has even been introduced at some stores. But none of this seems to have stemmed demand, as shoppers have descended on retailers in the hopes of snagging whatever stock they have.

Retailers taking advantage of this include GameStop, which is selling the $49.99 Elite Trainer Box of cards for $169.99, a stunt it has pulled previously. Dick's Sporting Goods, meanwhile, has the same package for a slightly cheaper $119.99 (thanks, Polygon ) — still more than double the upfront cost).

Long queues have been spotted this morning in both the U.K. and France, where the cards are now on sale. Numerous fans pitched up tents or slept on camping chairs to keep their spot in the queue:

A huge queue outside The Entertainer in Altrincham this morning as Pokémon fans wait to get their hands on a special release of trading cards marking the game’s 30th birthday. On the other side of the Atlantic, lines of fans outside stores began several days ago in some locations. There has also been criticism of people reserving their spot with so-called 'ghost chairs' — essentially leaving a seat in place to mark a spot, days in advance.

The idea here is that you are forming a line of chairs that are then left empty, days before the thing you are actually lining up for. On the one hand, it's a practice that will save a lot of people from several uncomfortable days parked out on the street. On the other, it hardly seems fair to those who do turn up on the day of release to a row of empty seats in front of them.

What happens if you turn up to queue — potentially overnight — and there are already chairs in front? Being there in person, do you get priority over a 'ghost chair' spot reserved by someone who is not? It is situations like these that are likely to prompt the squabbles that often break out during such gatherings ahead of product launches, especially if you've been left grumpy by a night in the cold.

New card releases frequently sell out completely, and The Pokémon Company has appeared unable or unwilling to fully keep up with demand — despite a staggering 10 billion cards printed last year alone .

Earlier this week, one millionaire Pokémon collector suggested that the cards will likely be used as currency following a global apocalypse . Looking to start your collection? articles.title: Netflix Reveals Narnia: The Magician's Nephew Logo as Theatrical and Streaming Release Dates Approach
articles.summary: Netflix has revealed its logo for Narnia: The Magician's Nephew, the upcoming fantasy blockbuster directed by Barbie's Greta Gerwig.
articles.body:
Netflix has revealed its logo for Narnia: The Magician's Nephew , the upcoming fantasy blockbuster directed by Barbie's Greta Gerwig.

For almost three months, the Netflix-made Narnia will be exclusive to theaters from its release on February 12, with IMAX previews beginning on February 10. Netflix subscribers will then be able to stream the movie, but only from April 2 onwards.

While Netflix has given short theatrical windows to a few other films, this extended period is extremely unusual. Martin Scorsese's The Irishman was available via limited theatrical release for less than a month, while Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery had just a single week in theaters before it dropped onto Netflix.

The Magician's Nephew is chronologically the first book in C. S. Lewis' beloved Narnia series , though most adaptations to date have begun with The Lion, The Witch and The Wardrobe — the first Narnia story published, and by far the most famous. Indeed, The Magician's Nephew has never been adapted for the screen until now.

Clearly, though, Netflix hopes that this fresh entry point into the franchise will be a successful start to its plans for the series, with an all-star cast and years of work to bring the story to life. Carey Mulligan, Daniel Craig, Emma Mackey, Ciarán Hinds and Meryl Streep all feature in the film, with its young leads played by newcomers David McKenna and Beatrice Campbell.

Don't expect Netflix to make theatrical releases the norm for its movies in future, however. Netflix film boss Dan Lin recently said that the streamer "just won't work with" filmmakers who push to bring their films to the big screen — with Gerwig seemingly a notable exception.

articles.title: Crackdown Was So Much More Than Just the Halo 3 Beta’s Pack-In Game
articles.summary: The original Crackdown turned out to be a really terrific comic-book power fantasy brought to life. Or, put another way, a game very worthy of any Xbox 360 owner’s attention, regardless of the fact that it was a surrogate for the public’s first taste of Halo 3.
articles.body:
This is an IGN opinion piece from Ryan McCaffrey, who worked at Official Xbox Magazine from 2002-2012 during the original Xbox and Xbox 360 era before joining IGN, where he remains “the Xbox guy.” In the run-up to Xbox’s 25th anniversary, he’ll be sharing his memories from the platform’s first quarter-century.

Crackdown 2 just didn’t hit. It was a pretty same-y sequel that didn’t bring a lot of appealing new stuff to the table, aside from four-player co-op. And Crackdown 3? Well, the development of that one might be more interesting than the final game itself turned out to be. Remember when the Xbox’s Azure servers in the cloud were going to power a fully destructible world? The power of countless Xbox Ones, all working together – gaming’s first data center (I’m only half-joking)! The promise of what Crackdown 3 said it was going to do versus what it finally delivered in the end was, well…let’s just say there was a Grand Canyon-sized gap that not even a fully powered-up Crackdown Agent could leap across.

But the original Crackdown? That one, funny enough, was almost the opposite. No one necessarily expected much from it at all (though in hindsight, we probably should have, given who was overseeing it – more on that in a moment). It was discounted as The Thing You Had to Buy to Get the Halo 3 Multiplayer Beta . It’s true; the PS2 had Zone of the Enders as its Metal Gear Solid 2 delivery system, and the Xbox 360 used a new IP of its own to bring Crackdown to the masses in an age just before digital delivery really took over for these kinds of things.

It turned out to be a really terrific comic-book power fantasy brought to life . Or, put another way, a game very worthy of any Xbox 360 owner’s attention, regardless of the fact that it was a surrogate for the public’s first taste of Halo 3. Set in Pacific City, three gangs had taken over different areas of town, and it was up to you as a fledgling Agent to stop them. You’d get better at running, shooting, and driving by doing those activities. Kill an enemy with a gun and a pile of gun skill orbs would explode out of him. Same with agility (jumping), strength (melee attacks), explosives (using grenades or rocket launchers), and driving. Eventually you could almost literally leap tall buildings in a single bound. In fact, I’d go so far as to say that Crackdown has one of the most satisfying power progressions in a game that I’ve ever played (I’d also put the underappreciated original-Xbox cult classic Breakdown in this group too). In the beginning of the game you can run a bit, shoot a bit, punch a bit, drive a bit, and jump a bit. By the end, if you’d put all the work in at the gym known as the entirety of Pacific City, you were a fully fledged superhero.

Extra cool at the time was that Crackdown didn’t put any guardrails on where you could and couldn’t go. The leaders of the city’s gangs were waiting for you in their strongholds. Sure, they were heavily guarded by minions and underlings, but if you could figure out a way through and kill the gang leader in the first hour or two of the game, then more power to you!

Crackdown also has, to this day, some of my all-time favorite Xbox Achievements. The most memorable of these were tied together: there was the “High Flyer” Achievement for climbing your way to the very top of Agency Tower, the tallest building in the city. And then, if you successfully jumped off and splashed down in the adjacent bay without faceplanting into the pavement immediately surrounding the Tower, you’d get the “Base Jumper” Achievement.

As I mentioned before, Crackdown being a sneaky-great open-world superhero power fantasy shouldn’t have been a surprise, as it was directed by David Jones, aka the Original Creator of Grand Theft Auto. While Jones hadn’t worked on Rockstar’s megafranchise in quite some time, he nevertheless helped get it off the ground, and thus clearly knew a thing or two about building a great sandbox.

It’s a bummer that Microsoft could never quite recapture the magic of the original Crackdown, and in all likelihood the series is probably done for good, what with Asha Sharma’s franchise-first focus for the company moving forward, but Crackdown was a highlight in an Xbox 360 era full of highlights, and it deserves to be remembered for being more than just a necessary purchase to get your hands on the Halo 3 multiplayer beta.

Ryan McCaffrey is IGN's executive editor of previews and host of IGN's weekly Xbox show, Podcast Unlocked , and a co-host of Next-Gen Console Watch . He's a North Jersey guy, so it's "Taylor ham," not "pork roll." Debate it with him on Twitter at @DMC_Ryan .

articles.title: Save $10 on Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave for Nintendo Switch 2
articles.summary: Today is your last chance to save $10 on a physical copy of Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave for Nintendo Switch 2.
articles.body:
Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave comes out tomorrow for Nintendo Switch 2. That means today is your last chance to save $10 off physical copies of the game at Amazon and Walmart . In case you’re wondering if the game is any good, you can hop over to our 10/10 review to see what our critic thought of it. But for real, if you want a physical copy, grab one today, because it goes back up to $79.99 tomorrow.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave for $10 Off (Ends Today)

Digital copies are $69.99 on the Nintendo eShop , and will be for the foreseeable future. But earlier this year, Nintendo started charging $10 more for physical games versus digital, presumably because physical cartridges and printing and shipping cost more than serving up downloads of data.

In response to this pricing change, both Amazon and Walmart have gone rogue among retailers and begun offering $10 off preorders of physical copies, bringing the pricing in line with digital copies. But once the game comes out, the price goes back up to MSRP – $79.99, in this case.

Generally, preordering can be a risky move because you don’t always know if a game is worth buying before reviews hit, or it comes out and gets a popular consensus. But right now, we’re in a beautiful window of time when reviews are live and the game is still discounted on Amazon and Walmart. But, again, today is the last day.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is the latest in a long line of tactical RPGs that provide anime-inspired art and stories, turn-based strategy gameplay, and deep character interactions. People love these games , and for good reason — they’re usually terrific.

Looks like this one is no different. Here’s how IGN critic Brendan Graeber summed it up in the review:

“Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave builds upon its strategic arts in ways I couldn’t have anticipated. It’s never satisfied to make me grow only as a battlefield tactician, or only in my ability to manage my time between skirmishes wisely, but both in perfect harmony. Every time I turned around, I was being given more challenges to face and more tools to master in order to overcome them. The many unique twists of each hero’s story path had me eager to see all the ways those journeys differed from each other, making the grand culmination in the final act hit so damn well. Planning out my expeditions across an imposing map became an unexpected highlight that not only hooked me, but rewarded my persistence by continuing to expand all the ways I could direct my armies as I tried to stay on top of newly emerging threats. The scope of both its formidably challenging battles and intricate management systems would be wildly ambitious for one path, let alone spread across four – yet somehow Fortune’s Weave only gets better and better each time you guide its captivating heroes into the colosseum and far beyond.”

articles.title: Collectors Rejoice: The Marvel Masterworks Line Is Making a Comeback in 2026
articles.summary: The beloved Marvel Masterworks line is making a comeback, as Clover Press continues the more than 20-year collecting journey.
articles.body:
For decades, the Marvel Masterworks line served as the gold standard for reprinting classic superhero comics in a comprehensive, collector-friendly format. That is, until Marvel finally shelved the Masterworks line at the beginning of 2026. Thankfully, Clover Press has stepped in to fill the void. They're reviving Marvel Masterworks and picking up right where Marvel itself left off.

Clover Press will be continuing the Marvel Masterworks line via crowdfunding. Their initial Kickstarter campaign focuses on four hardcovers - Marvel Masterworks: The Uncanny X-Men Vol. 18, Marvel Masterworks: Super-Villain Team-Up Vol. 1, Marvel Masterworks: The Mighty Thor Vol. 25, and Marvel Masterworks: The Tomb of Dracula Vol. 6. Each book will be available in one of three cover variants, two of which match the classic Masterworks formats and one that takes a new, more stylized approach.

Check out the slideshow gallery below for a closer look at the cover art for these books, as well as an exclusive preview of Marvel Masterworks: The Uncanny X-Men Vol. 18:

Marvel Masterworks Returns at Clover Press: Preview Gallery

As before, the goal with these Marvel Masterworks hardcovers is to provide a complete and chronological collection of classic Marvel Comics material, reprinted as close to the original art as possible. In some cases, the books have been painstakingly rescanned and restored from the original artwork. And Marvel Masterworks collectors will be happy to know that longtime series editor Cory Sedlmeier will continue to oversee the line.

Here's the official summary of these four books:

In Marvel Masterworks: The Uncanny X-Men, Vol. 18, Chris Claremont and Jim Lee begin their march towards X-Men #1, the Guiness Book of World Records top-selling comic book of all time—collecting THE UNCANNY X-MEN (1981) 256-268 & ANNUAL (1970) 14 and material from THE FANTASTIC FOUR ANNUAL (1963) 23, X-FACTOR ANNUAL (1986) 5 and THE NEW MUTANTS ANNUAL (1984) 6. Featuring an introduction by Chris Claremont

Featuring an introduction by Chris Claremont

In Marvel Masterworks: Super-Villain Team-Up, Vol. 1, Doctor Doom and his notorious accomplices Namor and the Red Skull take the stage in this classic Marvel series which gives the bad guys full rein—collecting GIANT-SIZE SUPER-VILLAIN TEAM-UP (1975) 1-2, SUPER-VILLAIN TEAM-UP (1975) 1-17, MARVEL SPOTLIGHT (1971) 27, THE AVENGERS (1963) 154-156, THE CHAMPIONS (1975) 16 and material from MARVEL PREVIEW (1975) 21. Featuring an introduction by Roy Thomas

In Marvel Masterworks: The Mighty Thor, Vol. 25, Walter Simonson and Sal Buscema’s original art is faithfully restored and looking better than ever as The God of Thunder leads an army into Hel itself in this fan-favorite classic every Marvel fan should have in their library—collecting THE MIGHTY THOR (1966) 360-369 and BALDER THE BRAVE (1985) 1-4. Featuring an introduction by Walter Simonson

Featuring an introduction by Walter Simonson

In Marvel Masterworks: The Tomb of Dracula, Vol. 6, high-stakes storytelling pulls long-running characters like Quincy Harker, Rachel van Helsing and Blade into a final reckoning that leaves no one untouched from collaborators Marv Wolfman, Gene Colan and Tom Palmer—collecting THE TOMB OF DRACULA (1972) 56-70. Featuring an introduction by Kelley Jones

Featuring an introduction by Kelley Jones

“Each Masterworks volume has a completely new restoration that outshines all past editions,” said Sedlmeier in a statement. “More than 40% of the final issue of Tomb of Dracula—an issue that suffered from poor reproduction in all past printings, including the original comic—has been restored from original art; dozens of pages of Jim Lee X-Men have been restored from the originals; and over 200 pages of Walter Simonson’s Thor have been restored from original art scans that Walter did just for this Masterworks. Coupled with the highest fidelity reproduction ever at 1200dpi and meticulous color restoration, the new line of Masterworks is going to knock the socks off readers old and new alike.”

The Kickstarter campaign for the new Marvel Masterworks line is live now. The campaign features plenty of optional bonuses like a Premium Works collector box, Fact Files character cards, journals, buttons, character stickers, mini prints, large artist edition prints, postcards, stationery-inspired inserts, facsimile posters, dustjackets, and die-cut slipcases.

articles.title: Wardogs Outpacing Arc Raiders and Helldivers 2 on Steam and Has Already Made More Money Than Marathon Across All Platforms to Date, Analysis Shows
articles.summary: Breakout hit Wardogs is outpacing Arc Raiders and Helldivers 2 on Steam in terms of copies sold at launch, new data shows.
articles.body:
Breakout hit Wardogs is outpacing Arc Raiders and Helldivers 2 on Steam in terms of copies sold at launch, new data shows.

Bulkhead’s tactical first-person shooter released in early access form on Steam on September 10 and hit a peak of 428,666 concurrent players soon after, becoming one of the most-played games on Valve’s platform. It sold 1 million copies on day one and 1.25 million by day two. Bulkhead announced 2 million sales after just five days .

According to Rhys Elliott of Alinea Analytics , Wardogs is now up to 2.2 million copies sold on Steam, which means it’s outpacing Arc Raiders (1.7 million) and Helldivers 2 (1 million) when launch aligned on Valve’s platform.

Not only that, with approximately $70 million in revenue generated so far, Wardogs has already made more money on Steam alone than Bungie’s Marathon has managed across PC and console so far, Elliott’s data suggests. “It’s another reminder that, when it comes to live-service games, community trumps budget and pedigree,” he said.

The question now is can Wardogs maintain its momentum with both Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 and GTA 6 around the corner. Both Arc Raiders and Helldivers 2 enjoyed huge interest months after release, and went on to sell many millions of copies. Wardogs still has a long way to go before matching both games longer term, but it’s worth remembering Wardogs is in early access, where it will remain for 1-2 years. A console version planned for 2028. “We are adamant that we do not want to be in Early Access for a long time,” its Steam page reads. Overnight, Bulkhead boss Joe Brammer said Season 2 will bring “lots of new content and changes” now Wardogs was entering the next phase of development.

“Wardogs‘ growth story is far from over,” Elliott continued. “It’s got some maintenance hills to climb and a strong roadmap to deliver on before it can dream of reaching the heights of, say, an Arc Raiders.

“But make no mistake: even if it never sold another copy, Wardogs is already a huge success. It’s a $40 shooter aimed at a slightly unfashionable audience that stuck to its guns and turned out bloody great.

“You can’t really replicate what Bulkhead pulled off here, but they knew exactly who the game was for, priced it fairly, built the community before launch (and actually talked to them), cut the PR nonsense, were authentic (to a fault at times), and made something cool.”

On that $40 price point, Elliott suggested Wardogs hit “the modern pricing sweet spot, sitting below the friction point of a $70 AAA release while capturing that chunky volume of players priced out of premium titles.”

User reviews are now ‘Very Positive’ after initial complaints around launch problems. That appears to be done and dusted now, with players getting on with the game and having fun. A number of gameplay clips showing Wardogs shenanigans have gone viral ( players are even avoiding Wardogs’ Lonestar faction over a perception that they seemingly attract the worst players and lose the most games ).

articles.title: 'I Might Just Quit It All and Make Anime the Rest of My Life' — Sinners Star Michael B. Jordan Has More Than One Anime Project in the Works
articles.summary: Michael B. Jordan is currently working on more than one anime project, and even joked that he might leave Hollywood behind to focus on anime full-time.
articles.body:
Michael B. Jordan is currently working on more than one anime project, and even joked that he might leave Hollywood behind to focus on anime full-time.

It’s no secret that Michael B. Jordan is a huge anime fan. He’s been open about his love for iconic series like Dragon Ball , Hunter x Hunter , and Naruto , as well as famous films like Studio Ghibli’s Princess Mononoke . In fact, the last fight in Creed 3 was inspired by anime-style brawls, with the actor saying he took direct influence from boxing series Hajime no Ippo and Megalo Box . (Side note: If you haven’t watched Ippo, do yourself a favor and pull it up on Netflix right now.)

Now that Sinners has had some time to breathe, Jordan is diving into the anime world to make his own creations in the space, and even joked that he might ditch the world of traditional filmmaking to pursue his passion full time.

Jordan chatted about the subject in a cover interview for the October 2026 issue of Vogue , where the outlet revealed that he has “some [anime] projects in early stages of development.”

“I might just quit it all and make anime the rest of my life,” he told Vogue, with reporter Kelefa Sanneh remarking that he was “only half-joking.”

IGN got the chance to chat with Jordan back in February 2023, where he gushed about the anime that shaped Creed 3’s visual flair and combat sequences.

"Without nerding out too much... You've seen so many fights throughout the Rocky and Creed franchise, and I really wanted to put my spin on it, you know? How to make these fights different, and you know, from Hajime no Ippo, to Megalo Box, to Naruto, to My Hero Academia, all of those different anime that I watched growing up, there's an inherent spirit to them in how they fight..." he told us at IGN Fan Fest.

"And their bonds and relationships and all that good stuff. But it's very similar to the brotherhood and bond that we have, and his relationship to his family as well. So I tried to key in on some of those key moments. And yeah, they're in there. They're in a lot of the fights. …I would say from the Dragon Ball Z universe, there's a punch... [in] me and Damian's fight, where there's a Dragon Ball Z punch that's in there."

While it’s as-yet unclear what Jordan’s anime projects will be, fans can look forward to his performance alongside Austin Butler in Miami Vice '85 , a reboot of the iconic 80s TV series that’s set to release on August 6, 2027.

Jordan is also working on a Battlefield movie alongside Christopher McQuarrie, with the two stars reportedly shopping the adaptation around to different studios in hopes of bringing Electronic Arts’ popular military game series to the silver screen.
