articles.title: An Iconic Iron Man #1 Page and Other Historic Comic Book Art Head to Auction
articles.summary: If you have Tony Stark levels of money, you can now own one of the most iconic and important pieces of Iron Man art ever published.
articles.body:
Heritage Auctions has revealed a new lineup of classic comic book artwork included in the upcoming Comic Art Signature Auction event, and there are truly some doozies. Among them is an iconic page from 1968's Iron Man #1, originally owned by none other than Marvel Studios founding chairman David Maisel.

The art in question is the opening splash page from that issue, making it the very first piece of art from the very first solo Iron Man comic. The art was created by penciller Gene Colan and inker Johnny Craig. Check it out below:

Unsurprisingly, owning a true piece of comic book history like this won't come cheap. The page is currently up for auction , with the price as of the time of publish already reaching a whopping $6,750.

“Gene created two things,” Maisel said in a press release. “He made the suit expressive and almost limber, and he was very cinematic in his art, and almost foreseeing the MCU at some point in time, almost 40 years later. The combination of it being the historic first page of the first issue, the big art of a Page 1 splash, the fun ‘What a way to start out in your own mag’ and Gene’s art was something I couldn’t say no to.”

There are several other historic pages featured in this auction event. One is artist Jerry Robinson's cover to 1942's Detective Comics #68 . Not only is that issue the second appearance of Two-Face, the sheer fact that a piece of original art from the Golden Age has survived in such good shape is pretty notable. The same goes for Joe Shuster's cover to 1940's Action Comics #22 .

Other noteworthy listings include several pages from Frank Miller's seminal Daredevil run from the 1980s and Jim Lee's cover to 1992's X-Men #6 (which is currently bidding at an eye-watering $135,000). Clearly, collecting original comic art is not a hobby for the frugal.

Would you like to bid on this Iron Man #1 page or any of the other art featured above? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title: A Misfire for Marvel: DNX #1 Fails to Deliver as the High-Stakes X-Men and Fantastic Four Crossover Event Falls Flat in an Uninspired Debut Issue
articles.summary: Marvel's latest crossover event is off to a bland start, as DNX #1 fails to make the most of the latest alliance between the X-Men and Fantastic Four.
articles.body:
Try as I might, I've had a very difficult time connecting with Marvel's current lineup of X-Men comics. At first, that sense of disconnect could be chalked up to the sting of losing the Krakoa status quo back in 2024. The Age of Krakoa was easily the most creatively fruitful period in the X-Men franchise since the heyday of Chris Claremont's run, and Marvel made a grave error in opting to wipe the slate clean rather than finding a way to move forward with the resilient mutant nation as the permanent baseline. But that apathy to the post-Krakoa X-Men line hasn't faded over the past two years. The X-Men franchise is stuck in a creative rut, and any hope that the DNX crossover will shake things loose is sadly dashed in the first issue.

DNX is ostensibly an X-Men/Fantastic Four crossover event, though its roots lie mainly in writer Jed MacKay's ongoing X-Men series and last year's Age of Revelation crossover. The premise behind the series is that both Cyclops and White Beast (the original, corrupted version of Hank McCoy who now leads the supervillain cabal known as 3K) have seen the future where a devastating virus has transformed humanity into mutants. Cyclops seeks to prevent that future from coming to pass, while White Beast wants to own that future. And now the simmering conflict between the X-Men and 3K comes to a head.

Frankly, I wish this issue were as efficient in laying out the scope of the conflict. But instead, the script gets very bogged down by exposition right from the get-go. There's too much emphasis on Cyclops explaining the stakes and summarizing recent X-events and not nearly enough on diving into the actual conflict. The result is that the story barely feels like it's gotten started by the time issue #1 reaches its end. With Marvel already in the midst of multiple other crossover events at the moment (Avengers: Armageddon and Queen in Black), DNX really needed to make a stronger case for itself starting out.

It doesn't help that the FF characters feel so superfluous here. They enter the story via a subplot involving regular Beast turning to Mister Fantastic to cure Magneto of his ongoing genetic malady. Even with that storytelling vector, it never feels like the Fantastic Four have a logical or organic reason for being a part of this conflict. This reads more like a regular arc of MacKay's X-Men run with an outside super-team shoehorned in. 2012's Age of Ultron showed there is potential in exploring the unlikely partnership between mutants and the Richards family (in the case, the Wolverine/Invisible Woman alliance), so hopefully DNX will eventually find some interesting veins to mine there.

DNX #1 only really works when it focuses on the 3K characters. Any team that forces characters like Cassandra Nova and Magneto's clone Joseph to work to work together is bound to be a flimsy arrangement at best, and McKay makes the most of that here. You almost have to feel sorry for White Beast as he sees his back-stabbing, deceitful allies snatching defeat from the jaws of victory and tries to hold the entire enterprise together through sheer force of will.

Artist Federico Vicentini and colorist David Curiel do their best to spice up what is a very dialogue-heavy first issue. Vicetini's figure work is inconsistent at best, particularly when it comes to character faces, but he does bring a palpable energy to the page that helps offset the plodding script. Maybe that comes at the expense of a few too many Dutch angle panels, but so be it. And Curiel's colors give everything a vivid look and feel, with some of the standout pages including a visual flashback to the Fatal Attractions crossover and the psyhcic battle between Quentin Quire and Cassandra Nova.

articles.title: The MSI Codex Z2C  RTX 5070 Prebuilt Gaming PC Drops to $1399 and Includes an Upcoming PC Game
articles.summary: Excellent prebuilt option for 1080p and 1440p gaming, and it's capable enough to run games in 4K as well.
articles.body:
B&H Photo is offering a solid deal on a prebuilt desktop computer that excels at 1080p and 1440p gaming. For a limited time you can pick up a brand new MSI Codex Z2C RTX 5070 gaming PC for just $1,399 with free shipping. The system comes with a download voucher for the upcoming Control: Resonant game, which comes out on September 22. Redemption instructions are found on Nvidia's website .

The MSI Codex Z2C RTX 5070 Gaming PC Drops to $1399

MSI Codex Z2C AMD Ryzen 7 8700F RTX 5070 Gaming PC (16GB/1TB)

The MSI Codex Z2C gaming PC is equipped with an AMD Ryzen 7 8700F CPU, GeForce RTX 5070 12GB GPU, 16GB of DDR5 RAM, and a 1TB M.2 SSD. The Ryzen 7 8700F is an 8-core, 16-thread processor with a max boost clock of 5.1GHz. It's not the fastest or newest AMD CPU, but it's still a solid gaming CPU that won't bottleneck the GPU, especially at the higher resolutions you should be playing at if you own a 5070 Ti. A 750W PSU powers the system.

The GeForce RTX 5070 GPU is an excellent choice for 1080p or 1440p gaming

The GeForce RTX 5070 is the best Nvidia card for 1080p and 1440p gaming and by itself this card retails for $600 (although generally it's higher these days). It's also powerful enough to run most games at 4K, although at that point you'll see noticeable gains jumping up to a 5070 Ti. Compared to the previous generation GPUs, the RTX 5070 offers a slight performance improvement over the RTX 4070 Super, which was and still is an excellent GPU. The fps gain is greater in games that support DLSS 4.5 with multi-frame generation. Check out our RTX 5070 review .

Eric Song is the IGN commerce manager in charge of finding the best gaming and tech deals every day. When Eric isn't hunting for deals for other people at work, he's hunting for deals for himself during his free time.

articles.title: Humble’s Isometric Immersion CRPG Pack Gets You 11 Exciting Games for Just $23
articles.summary: Humble’s Isometric Immersion CRPG Pack includes 11 games that have a total value of $291, but you can grab them all for your PC library for as low as $23.
articles.body:
If your Steam library is in need of some new PC games to play this fall, Humble's impressive Isometric Immersion CRPG Pack is worth checking out. In total, it comes with 11 games - including big hits like Disco Elysium: The Final Cut and Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader - that have a total cost of $291, but you can snag them all for as low as $23.

That's an incredible offer to be able to add all of these games - which you can see fully listed out below - to your Steam library. The bundle won't be available for long, though. Humble's store page states that it comes to an end in 7 days, so you only have a week left to add these new adventures to your PC library.

Humble Bundle – CRPG Pack: Isometric Immersion

As with many other bundles from Humble, you can actually choose how much you'd like to spend on it, though there are some changes that come into play. If you pay $15 instead, you'll get 9 games from the bundle rather than the full 11, which are: Pathfinder: Wrath of the Righteous, SKALD: Against the Black Priory, Black Geyser: Couriers of Darkness, Black Geyser: Couriers of Darkness - Tales of the Moon Cult, Torment: Tides of Numenera, Gamedec, Disco Elysium, UnderRail, and Balrum.

If you decide to drop even lower to $10, then you'll get five games: Torment: Tides of Numenera, Gamedec, Disco Elysium, UnderRail, and Balrum. So, if you're hoping to get all 11, $23 is as low as you can go. On the other hand, if you're feeling generous, you can opt to pay a little extra as well, which gets you all 11 games and gives more to publishers, Humble, and charity. The latter for this bundle is Little Free Library .

Quite a few of the games here have earned high marks from us as well, so it's exciting to see them all in one big bundle. Disco Elysium: The Final Cut was a solid 10/10 in our review , while both Rogue Trader and Pathfinder: Wrath of the Righteous earned 8s in their respective reviews. Torment: Tides of Numenera even inched above those with a score of 8.8, so there's plenty of great options to keep you entertained.

Again, though, this bundle only has 7 days left before it comes to an end. Be quick to grab it before it's all gone.

Humble Bundle is part of IGN Entertainment, the division of Ziff Davis that includes GamesIndustry.biz, IGN, and MapGenie.

Hannah Hoolihan is a freelancer who writes with the guides and commerce teams here at IGN.
